1: key factors in a visualization project
The eight hats of data visualization design
2: Using visual analysis to find stories

questions.t: The eight hats of data visualization design
questions.q: In the eight hats of data visualization design, which role focuses on how visual choices affect human perception, attention and memory?
questions.model: The cognitive scientist brings knowledge of perception and cognition to design decisions.

questions.q: Distinguish visualizations whose function is to explain, to explore and to exhibit, giving one example of each from university admissions data.
questions.model: Explain: the designer leads the reader to a finding (annotated chart showing that applications doubled after a new programme). Explore: the user investigates freely (interactive filters by state and programme). Exhibit: data shown for reference without a narrative (a table of seats per course).

questions.q: True or False: Metaphor visualization organises abstract information using a familiar visual structure, such as a map, a tree or a road, to aid understanding.
questions.model: True; the metaphor transfers the reader's understanding of a familiar structure to the information.

questions.t: key factors in a visualization project
questions.q: List four key factors that should be settled at the start of a visualization project and explain how one of them constrains design choices.
questions.model: Purpose/intent, audience, data availability and quality, format and medium, time and resources. Example: a printed annual report cannot use interactivity, so annotation and arrangement must carry the message.

questions.q: Explain how the physical properties of data (categorical, ordinal or quantitative values; range and distribution) influence the choice of visual encoding, with one example each.
questions.model: Categorical: distinct hues or positions, no implied order (product types). Ordinal: ordered positions or sequential colour (grades A-E). Quantitative: position or length on a scale (sales). A wide or skewed range may need a log scale or binning (city populations).

questions.q: Which visual encoding allows readers to compare quantitative values most accurately?
questions.model: Perception studies rank position on a common aligned scale as the most accurately judged encoding.

questions.q: A monthly fee-collection line chart is to be shown to the finance committee. Suggest three annotations and one arrangement decision that would make its message clear.
questions.model: Annotate the target line, label the lowest month with its cause (e.g. a portal outage), and add a short headline stating the trend. Arrangement: place the chart first with supporting breakdowns below, aligned to the same time axis.

questions.t: Using visual analysis to find stories
questions.q: Describe how you would use visual analysis to find stories in the case data, which views you would build first, and how you would turn one finding into a narrative for the public.
questions.case: A city has hourly air-quality readings (PM2.5, PM10, NO2) from 25 monitoring stations for three years, with station locations, traffic counts and dates of festivals and policy changes.
questions.model: Start with distributions and time series per pollutant, small multiples by station, a map of station averages, and scatter plots of PM2.5 against traffic. Look for seasonality, outliers (festival spikes), before/after policy changes. Build a narrative: question, evidence (annotated time series and map), context, conclusion, with clear caveats on data gaps.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about the choropleth map and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A choropleth map should usually show rates or densities rather than raw totals.
questions.reason: Larger or more populous regions accumulate larger totals, which distorts comparisons between regions.
questions.model: Both true and R explains A: normalising (per capita, per km2) makes regions comparable.

questions.q: Which chart is designed to show a stock's daily open, high, low and close prices over time?
questions.model: A candlestick chart encodes open, high, low and close for each period.

questions.q: A department's budget is split into 6 schools and 30 sub-heads. Evaluate a pie chart and a treemap for showing this hierarchy and recommend one.
questions.model: A pie chart handles only a few slices and one level; 30 sub-heads would be unreadable and angles are judged poorly. A treemap shows both levels, scales to many items and uses area within nested rectangles. Recommend the treemap, with labels for the largest items.

questions.q: Explain what a scatter plot matrix shows and how you would use it to examine the relationships among attendance, internal marks, assignment scores and end-semester marks.
questions.model: A grid of scatter plots of every pair of variables (with distributions on the diagonal). Scan it for correlations (e.g. internal vs end-semester marks), clusters and outliers, then examine strong pairs in detail.

questions.q: Evaluate Tableau, Google Charts and Datawrapper for two needs: (a) a newsroom publishing quick charts on its website, and (b) an enterprise sales team needing interactive dashboards over several data sources. Recommend a tool for each.
questions.model: (a) Datawrapper: browser-based, fast, publication-ready charts and maps without code; Google Charts suits teams with web developers. (b) Tableau: connects to many sources, blending, interactive dashboards, sharing. Recommend Datawrapper for (a) and Tableau for (b).

questions.q: Google Charts is best described as:
opts: A JavaScript library for embedding interactive charts in web pages
A database for storing chart data
questions.model: Charts are created in JavaScript and rendered in the browser.

questions.q: True or False: Datawrapper lets users create publication-ready charts and maps in a web browser without writing code.
questions.model: True; it is a browser-based tool aimed at quick, publishable charts and maps.

questions.q: List four criteria you would use to select a data visualization tool for a university department.
questions.model: Supported data sources and data size; interactivity and sharing options; ease of use and training needed; cost and licensing; security and data-privacy controls.

questions.q: Compare a join and data blending in Tableau: when is each performed, at what level of detail, and when would you choose blending?
questions.model: A join combines tables row by row in the data source before aggregation. Blending queries each source separately, aggregates at the view's level of detail, then combines on linking fields (like a left join of aggregates). Choose blending for different databases or different granularities, e.g. monthly targets against daily sales.

questions.q: Quarterly sales are Q1 = 20, Q2 = 30, Q3 = 25 and Q4 = 25. What value does a 'percent of total' table calculation show for Q2?
In Tableau, what does a FIXED level-of-detail expression such as {FIXED [Region] : SUM([Sales])} compute?
opts: Sales at whatever dimensions are in the view
Sales per region, regardless of the dimensions in the view
A running total across all regions
The average of sales across regions
questions.model: FIXED computes the aggregate at the dimensions listed, independent of the view.

questions.q: Design an interactive Tableau dashboard for admissions staff to monitor applications by programme, state and week. Specify the views, filters, dashboard actions and one dual-axis chart, and explain how the design supports the staff's decisions.
questions.model: Views: KPI cards (applications, offers, conversion), weekly applications line with offers on a dual axis, map by state, bar chart by programme. Filters: session, programme type. Actions: clicking a state filters the other views; hovering highlights a programme. The dual axis compares applications and offer rate over time, showing where follow-up is needed.
